Relies on fₛ,max being proportional to N with μₛ independent of load (the empirical friction model)
practice.why: The same cancellation makes \( a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta) \) independent of mass.

practice.prompt: A 2.00 kg block rests on top of a 5.00 kg block on a frictionless floor; \( \mu_s = 0.400 \) between the blocks. A horizontal force pulls the lower block. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², what is the largest force, in newtons, for which the blocks move together?
practice.why: The upper block is accelerated only by static friction: \( ma \le \mu_s mg \Rightarrow a \le \mu_s g = 3.92 \) m/s². Moving together, \( F = (m + M)a \le (7.00)(3.92) = 27.4 \) N.

options: doubles, because the pressure on the smaller face is twice as large
halves, because the contact area is halved
stays the same, because it depends only on \( \mu_k \) and \( N \)
depends on the sliding speed, so it cannot be determined
practice.prompt: A crate slides across a floor on its largest face. It is turned onto a face with half the area (same mass, same materials) and slides at the same speed. According to the standard friction model, the kinetic friction force
practice.why: \( f_k = \mu_k N \), and \( N = mg \) is unchanged, so the friction is the same: to a good approximation friction does not depend on the apparent contact area. Options 1 and 2 reason from pressure or area, which the model says do not matter (the true microscopic contact area tracks the load, not the face size). Option 4 contradicts the approximate speed-independence of kinetic friction, and the speed is the same anyway.

practice.prompt: A small object falls from rest with linear drag and time constant \( \tau = 0.0200 \) s. How long, in seconds, does it take to reach 90.0% of its terminal speed?

practice.model: A tire that rolls without skidding has its contact patch momentarily at rest on the road, so the road acts on it through static friction, whose maximum is \( \mu_s N \). A locked wheel skids, and the road acts through kinetic friction \( \mu_k N \). On a level road \( N = mg \) (for the car as a whole), so the largest decelerations are \( \mu_s g \) and \( \mu_k g \). From \( 0 = v_0^2 - 2ad \), the stopping distances are \( d_s = v_0^2/(2\mu_s g) \) with the wheels kept at the verge of skidding, and \( d_k = v_0^2/(2\mu_k g) \) with the wheels locked. Since \( \mu_s > \mu_k \) (about 1.0 versus 0.7 for rubber on dry concrete), \( d_s < d_k \). Anti-lock systems release and reapply the brakes rapidly to keep the tires near the static limit. (A further benefit, steering control, also comes from not skidding.)
practice.prompt: Anti-lock brakes prevent a car's wheels from locking. Using the friction model, explain why a car with anti-lock brakes can stop in a shorter distance than one whose wheels lock, and derive the stopping distance from speed \( v_0 \) on a level road in each case.
rubric: A rolling (non-skidding) tire is held by static friction at the contact patch; a locked, skidding tire by kinetic friction
Maximum braking force μₛmg exceeds μₖmg because μₛ > μₖ
Deceleration μg, so distance d = v₀²/(2μg): d = v₀²/(2μₛg) versus v₀²/(2μₖg)
The shorter distance is achieved at the verge of skidding (maximum static friction); the mass cancels
practice.why: The mass cancels in both distances; only the coefficients and \( v_0 \) matter.

practice.prompt: A 2.00 kg block is held at rest on a frictionless \( 30.0^\circ \) incline by a horizontal force. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², find the magnitude of that force, in newtons.
practice.why: Along the slope, the horizontal force's component \( F\cos 30.0^\circ \) (up the slope) balances \( mg\sin 30.0^\circ \) (down): \( F = mg\tan 30.0^\circ = 19.6(0.577) = 11.3 \) N. Perpendicular: \( N = mg\cos 30.0^\circ + F\sin 30.0^\circ = 22.6 \) N, larger than \( mg\cos\theta \).

practice.prompt: A block slides up a rough incline of angle \( \theta \) (type `theta`) with kinetic coefficient \( \mu \) (type `mu`). Give the magnitude of its acceleration in terms of \( g \), \( \theta \) and \( \mu \).
practice.why: Moving up the slope, both the weight component \( mg\sin\theta \) and friction \( \mu mg\cos\theta \) point down the slope: \( a = g(\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta) \).

practice.model: (a) With \( u = gt/v_t \), \( \dfrac{dv}{dt} = v_t\,\mathrm{sech}^2(u)\,\dfrac{g}{v_t} = g\big(1 - \tanh^2 u\big) = g\Big(1 - \dfrac{v^2}{v_t^2}\Big) \). Multiplying by \( m \) and using \( m g/v_t^2 = D \): \( m\,\dfrac{dv}{dt} = mg - Dv^2 \). Also \( v(0) = v_t\tanh 0 = 0 \). (b) For \( 0 \le v < v_t \) the net force \( mg - Dv^2 \) is positive, so the body keeps speeding up, but the net force, and hence the acceleration, shrinks to zero as \( v \to v_t \). The speed can therefore approach \( v_t \) but not pass it: at \( v = v_t \) the net force is zero, and the solution \( \tanh u < 1 \) for every finite \( u \) confirms that \( v_t \) is only approached asymptotically.
practice.prompt: (a) Verify by differentiation that \( v(t) = v_t\tanh(gt/v_t) \), with \( v_t = \sqrt{mg/D} \), solves \( m\,dv/dt = mg - Dv^2 \) with \( v(0) = 0 \). (b) Explain qualitatively why the speed approaches \( v_t \) but never exceeds it for a body dropped from rest.
rubric: Uses d/dx tanh x = 1 − tanh² x (sech² x)
dv/dt = g(1 − tanh²(gt/vₜ)) = g(1 − v²/vₜ²)
Multiplying by m and using D = mg/vₜ² gives mg − Dv²; v(0) = vₜ tanh 0 = 0
(b) While v < vₜ the net force mg − Dv² is positive but shrinks to 0 as v → vₜ; since tanh < 1, v stays below vₜ (at v = vₜ the net force vanishes)
practice.why: Both drag laws give the same qualitative picture; they differ in how fast \( v_t \) is approached.

phy-0-3.scope: The static and kinetic friction model, deciding whether a body slides, forces applied at an angle and the optimal pulling angle, inclined planes with and without friction, the critical angle, connected and stacked bodies with friction, and speed-dependent fluid drag with terminal speed; the energy dissipated by friction is left to the energy chapters, and rolling resistance is mentioned only qualitatively.

sections.md:
This section states the model of friction used throughout introductory mechanics and explains what kind of force each part of it describes.

**The contact force, resolved.** When two surfaces touch, each exerts a contact force on the other. Its component perpendicular to the surfaces is the normal force of the previous chapter; its component along the surfaces is **friction**. Two regimes behave differently: surfaces that do not slide relative to each other, and surfaces that do.

**Static friction.** While there is no relative sliding, the friction force is **static friction** \( \vec f_s \). Experiment, going back to Amontons (1699) and Coulomb (1781), shows that it can take any magnitude up to a maximum proportional to the normal force:
\[ f_s \le \mu_s N. \]
The dimensionless constant \( \mu_s \) is the **coefficient of static friction** of the pair of surfaces. Static friction is a constraint force, like the normal force: within its limit it takes exactly the value that prevents sliding, and that value comes from Newton's second law. Its direction opposes the sliding that would occur without it. The equality \( f_s = \mu_s N \) holds only at the threshold of slipping, a condition called **impending motion**.

**Kinetic friction.** Once the surfaces slide, the friction force is **kinetic friction** \( \vec f_k \), of magnitude
\[ f_k = \mu_k N, \]
directed opposite to the velocity of the body relative to the surface it slides on. The **coefficient of kinetic friction** \( \mu_k \) is usually smaller than \( \mu_s \), which is why a heavy piece of furniture is easier to keep moving than to start. Unlike static friction, kinetic friction is given by a formula and does not adjust to the other forces.

**Status of the model.** These are approximate empirical rules, not fundamental laws. Within their range of validity the friction force is roughly independent of the apparent area of contact, and kinetic friction is roughly independent of the sliding speed. A common explanation is that surfaces touch only at microscopic high points whose true total contact area grows in proportion to the load; this is a model, and the microscopic origin of friction is still an active field of research. Coefficients depend on the materials and on the condition of the surfaces (dry, wet, lubricated, polished), so tabulated values are rough: about 1.0 (static) and 0.7 (kinetic) for rubber on dry concrete, 0.5 and 0.3 for wood on wood, about 0.04 for Teflon on steel. A rolling wheel that does not skid is held by static friction, since its contact point is momentarily at rest on the road; the small resistance to rolling is a separate effect not treated here.

**Worked example.** A 20.0 kg crate rests on a level floor with \( \mu_s = 0.500 \) and \( \mu_k = 0.400 \). You push horizontally with a slowly increasing force \( F \). The normal force is \( N = mg = 196 \) N, so the maximum static friction is \( \mu_s N = 98.0 \) N.

1. \( F = 30.0 \) N: the crate stays at rest, so the second law requires \( f_s = 30.0 \) N, opposite the push, within the limit.
2. \( F = 90.0 \) N: still at rest, with \( f_s = 90.0 \) N.
3. \( F \) just above 98.0 N: static friction cannot grow further, and the crate starts to slide.
4. Sliding with \( F = 120 \) N: \( f_k = \mu_k N = 78.4 \) N, so \( a = (120 - 78.4)/20.0 = 2.08 \) m/s².

The plot shows the friction force (N) against the applied push (N) for this crate: friction equals the push up to 98.0 N, then drops to the constant kinetic value 78.4 N.

```plot
x: 0, 150
y: 0, 110
xlabel: applied force F (N)
ylabel: friction f (N)
f: x <= 98 ? x : 78.4 | friction on the crate
hline: 98 | maximum static friction
```

**Common mistakes.** Writing \( f_s = \mu_s N \) for a body at rest; that is only the maximum. Assuming that friction always opposes a body's motion: it opposes relative sliding between the surfaces, and a box on the floor of an accelerating truck is carried forward by static friction.

questions.prompt: A 12.0 kg box rests on a level floor with \( \mu_s = 0.600 \) and \( \mu_k = 0.450 \). You push it horizontally with 50.0 N. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², what is the magnitude of the friction force on the box, in newtons?
questions.why: Maximum static friction: \( \mu_s mg = 0.600(12.0)(9.80) = 70.6 \) N. The push, 50.0 N, is below this, so the box stays at rest and the second law gives \( f_s = 50.0 \) N. Answering 70.6 N treats the maximum as the actual value; answering \( \mu_k mg = 52.9 \) N uses kinetic friction for a body that is not sliding.

questions.model: Static friction acts only when the surfaces are not sliding, and its role is to keep them from sliding. Like the normal force, it is a constraint force: it takes whatever magnitude the second law requires to maintain the no-slip condition, up to a maximum \( \mu_s N \) that depends on the surfaces. A crate at rest pushed with 30 N has 30 N of static friction; pushed with 60 N, it has 60 N. So the model can only bound it, hence the inequality, with equality only at impending motion. Its direction opposes the relative sliding that would occur without it. Kinetic friction acts when the surfaces already slide; there is no constraint to maintain, and experimentally its magnitude is approximately \( \mu_k N \) regardless of the other forces, directed opposite the relative velocity. Hence an equation.
questions.prompt: Explain why static friction is described by an inequality, \( f_s \le \mu_s N \), while kinetic friction is described by an equation, \( f_k = \mu_k N \). In your answer say how the actual value and direction of static friction are determined.
rubric: Static friction is a constraint force: it takes whatever value prevents relative sliding
Its value is found from Newton's second law (e.g. equals the applied force for a body at rest); μₛN is only its maximum, reached at impending motion
Its direction opposes the sliding that would occur without it
Kinetic friction does not adjust: once sliding, its magnitude is fixed by μₖN and its direction is opposite the relative velocity
questions.why: Keeping 'maximum static friction' and 'actual static friction' distinct is the key to every friction problem.

sections.title: Static and kinetic friction

sections.md:
Because the value of static friction is not known in advance, a friction problem begins with a question: does the body slide? This section gives the procedure and applies it to forces applied at an angle, where friction and the normal force are coupled.

**Procedure.**

1. Assume no sliding. Draw the free-body diagram with an unknown static friction \( f_s \) along the surface and solve the second law, using the acceleration that the no-slip assumption implies, for the required \( f_s \) and for \( N \).
2. If \( |f_s| \le \mu_s N \), the assumption is consistent and the problem is solved.
3. If \( |f_s| > \mu_s N \), the assumption is false and the surfaces slide. Solve again with \( f_k = \mu_k N \) opposite the relative velocity.

The comparison uses the actual normal force, which is why \( N \) must come from the diagram rather than being assumed equal to \( mg \).

**Worked example.** The 20.0 kg crate of the previous section (\( \mu_s = 0.500 \), \( \mu_k = 0.400 \)) is now pulled by a rope with tension 95.0 N at \( 30.0^\circ \) above the horizontal. A horizontal push of 95.0 N would not move it (the limit was 98.0 N). Does the angled pull?

1. Assume rest. Vertical: \( N = mg - T\sin 30.0^\circ = 196 - 47.5 = 148.5 \) N. Horizontal: required \( f_s = T\cos 30.0^\circ = 82.3 \) N.
2. Limit: \( \mu_s N = 0.500(148.5) = 74.3 \) N, which is less than 82.3 N. The crate slides.
3. Sliding: \( f_k = 0.400(148.5) = 59.4 \) N, so \( a = (82.3 - 59.4)/20.0 = 1.14 \) m/s².

The rope's upward component lightens the load on the floor and so lowers the friction limit by more than the tilt reduces the horizontal pull.

**The best pulling angle.** For a pull \( F \) at angle \( \phi \) above the horizontal, sliding starts when \( F\cos\phi = \mu_s(mg - F\sin\phi) \), that is, when
\[ F(\phi) = \frac{\mu_s mg}{\cos\phi + \mu_s\sin\phi}. \]
Tilting the rope has two competing effects: it reduces the horizontal component, and it reduces \( N \) and hence the friction limit. To minimize \( F \), maximize the denominator \( h(\phi) = \cos\phi + \mu_s\sin\phi \). Setting \( h'(\phi) = -\sin\phi + \mu_s\cos\phi = 0 \) gives
\[ \tan\phi^* = \mu_s, \]
and \( h'' = -h < 0 \) there, so this is a maximum of \( h \). With \( \cos\phi^* = 1/\sqrt{1+\mu_s^2} \) and \( \sin\phi^* = \mu_s/\sqrt{1+\mu_s^2} \), \( h(\phi^*) = \sqrt{1 + \mu_s^2} \) and
\[ F_{\min} = \frac{\mu_s mg}{\sqrt{1 + \mu_s^2}}. \]
For the crate, \( \phi^* = \arctan 0.500 = 26.6^\circ \) and \( F_{\min} = 98.0/\sqrt{1.25} = 87.7 \) N, about 11% less than a horizontal pull. (The formula assumes the crate stays on the floor; here \( F\sin\phi^* = 39.2 \) N is well below \( mg \).)

In the plot, the curve is the force (N) needed to start the 196 N crate sliding, against the pulling angle \( \phi \) in degrees. Drag the slider \( k \), the value of \( \mu_s \), and watch the minimum move to the right, since it sits at \( \arctan\mu_s \).

```plot
x: 0, 80
y: 0, 250
xlabel: φ (degrees)
ylabel: F (N)
slider: k, 0.1, 1, 0.5 | μs
f: k*196/(cos(x*pi/180) + k*sin(x*pi/180)) | force needed to start sliding
```

**Common mistakes.** Using \( N = mg \) when the applied force has a vertical component. Forgetting that a push directed below the horizontal increases \( N \): then \( F = \mu_s mg/(\cos\phi - \mu_s\sin\phi) \), which grows without bound as \( \tan\phi \to 1/\mu_s \). Beyond that angle no push, however large, can start the crate.

questions.prompt: A 30.0 kg crate on a level floor has \( \mu_s = 0.400 \) and \( \mu_k = 0.300 \). It is pushed horizontally with 150 N. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², find the magnitude of its acceleration, in m/s² (enter 0 if it does not move).
questions.why: Test for rest: required \( f_s = 150 \) N, limit \( \mu_s mg = 0.400(294) = 117.6 \) N. The limit is exceeded, so the crate slides. \( f_k = 0.300(294) = 88.2 \) N and \( a = (150 - 88.2)/30.0 = 2.06 \) m/s².

questions.prompt: A crate of mass \( m \) on a level floor with static coefficient \( \mu \) (type `mu`) is pulled by a rope at the angle above the horizontal that minimizes the force needed to start it sliding. Give that minimum force in terms of \( \mu \), \( m \) and \( g \).
questions.why: At angle \( \phi \): \( F = \mu mg/(\cos\phi + \mu\sin\phi) \). The denominator is maximal where \( -\sin\phi + \mu\cos\phi = 0 \), i.e. \( \tan\phi = \mu \), where it equals \( \sqrt{1+\mu^2} \). So \( F_{\min} = \mu mg/\sqrt{1+\mu^2} \).

sections.title: Does it slide? Forces at an angle

sections.md:
An inclined plane is the simplest surface that is not horizontal, and it is where the choice of axes first matters. This section resolves the weight on an incline and solves the frictionless case.

**Choice of axes.** On an **inclined plane** at angle \( \theta \) above the horizontal, a body sliding on the surface accelerates along the surface. Take \( x \) along the incline (down the slope positive, unless the motion suggests otherwise) and \( y \) perpendicular to it. Then \( a_y = 0 \), the normal force lies along \( y \), friction (next section) lies along \( x \), and only the weight has to be resolved.

**Resolving the weight.** The perpendicular to the incline makes the angle \( \theta \) with the vertical: tilting the surface by \( \theta \) from the horizontal tilts its perpendicular by the same \( \theta \) from the vertical. So the weight has components
\[ w_x = mg\sin\theta \ \ (\text{down the slope}), \qquad w_y = -mg\cos\theta \ \ (\text{into the surface}). \]
Check the limits: at \( \theta = 0 \) the weight is entirely perpendicular to the surface (\( w_x = 0 \)); at \( \theta = 90^\circ \) it lies entirely along the now vertical surface (\( w_x = mg \)). Checking these two limits is the quickest way to catch a swapped sine and cosine.

**The frictionless incline.** With only the weight and the normal force acting,
\[ y:\ N - mg\cos\theta = 0 \ \Rightarrow\ N = mg\cos\theta, \qquad x:\ mg\sin\theta = ma \ \Rightarrow\ a = g\sin\theta. \]
The acceleration is independent of the mass and constant, so the constant-acceleration equations of one-dimensional kinematics apply along the incline. The normal force is less than the weight because the incline supports only the perpendicular component. Galileo exploited exactly this: on a gentle slope \( g\sin\theta \) is small, so the motion is slow enough to time, while its character (uniform acceleration) is the same as in free fall.

**Worked example.** A block is released from rest on a frictionless incline of \( 25.0^\circ \) and slides 3.00 m along it.

1. \( a = 9.80\sin 25.0^\circ = 4.14 \) m/s² down the slope.
2. Speed after 3.00 m: \( v = \sqrt{2ad} = \sqrt{2(4.14)(3.00)} = 4.98 \) m/s.
3. Time: \( t = \sqrt{2d/a} = \sqrt{6.00/4.14} = 1.20 \) s.

The block descends \( 3.00\sin 25.0^\circ = 1.27 \) m vertically, and \( \sqrt{2g(1.27)} \) is also 4.98 m/s: the speed is the same as after a free fall through the same height, though the time is longer. The energy chapters explain why.

**A body going up.** A block launched up a frictionless incline with speed \( v_0 \) has acceleration \( g\sin\theta \) directed down the slope throughout, so it travels \( d = v_0^2/(2g\sin\theta) \) along the incline before stopping, then slides back.

**Common mistakes.** Swapping sine and cosine; test with \( \theta \to 0 \). Resolving the normal force instead of the weight (with tilted axes the normal force is already along \( y \)). Writing \( N = mg\cos\theta \) when another force has a component perpendicular to the incline: a horizontal push \( F \) against a block on the incline gives \( N = mg\cos\theta + F\sin\theta \).

questions.prompt: A block is launched at 4.00 m/s up a frictionless incline of \( 20.0^\circ \). Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², how far along the incline does it travel before momentarily stopping, in meters?
questions.why: Along the incline the acceleration is \( g\sin 20.0^\circ = 3.35 \) m/s², directed down the slope. \( 0 = v_0^2 - 2ad \Rightarrow d = 16.0/(2 \times 3.35) = 2.39 \) m.

questions.model: The incline makes angle \( \theta \) with the horizontal. Rotating a line by \( \theta \) rotates its perpendicular by the same angle, so the perpendicular to the incline makes angle \( \theta \) with the vertical, which is the direction of the weight. The weight's component along the perpendicular is therefore \( mg\cos\theta \) (adjacent side) and its component along the slope, perpendicular to that, is \( mg\sin\theta \) (opposite side). Limits: on a horizontal surface (\( \theta = 0 \)) there is no tendency to slide, and indeed \( mg\sin 0 = 0 \) while the perpendicular component is the full \( mg \). On a vertical surface (\( \theta = 90^\circ \)) the body falls freely along the surface: \( mg\sin 90^\circ = mg \) and \( mg\cos 90^\circ = 0 \).
questions.prompt: Justify geometrically that on an incline of angle \( \theta \) the weight has components \( mg\sin\theta \) along the slope and \( mg\cos\theta \) perpendicular to it. Then explain how the limiting cases \( \theta = 0 \) and \( \theta = 90^\circ \) confirm which function goes with which component.
rubric: The perpendicular (normal direction) to the incline makes angle θ with the vertical, since rotating a line by θ rotates its perpendicular by θ
The weight is vertical, so its component along the normal direction is mg cos θ and along the slope mg sin θ
θ = 0: component along the slope must vanish (sin 0 = 0), perpendicular component is the full weight (cos 0 = 1)
θ = 90°: surface vertical, the whole weight lies along it (sin 90° = 1), none perpendicular
questions.why: The limit check takes seconds and catches the most common error in incline problems.

sections.title: The inclined plane

sections.md:
Adding friction to the incline answers two practical questions: at what angle does a resting body begin to slide, and how does friction change motion up and down the slope?

**A body at rest.** Use the axes of the previous section, with \( x \) down the slope and static friction \( f_s \) acting up the slope. With \( \vec a = \vec 0 \):
\[ y:\ N = mg\cos\theta, \qquad x:\ mg\sin\theta - f_s = 0 \ \Rightarrow\ f_s = mg\sin\theta. \]
The static friction is \( mg\sin\theta \), not \( \mu_s N \). The body stays at rest if this does not exceed the limit: \( mg\sin\theta \le \mu_s mg\cos\theta \), that is,
\[ \tan\theta \le \mu_s. \]
The **critical angle** \( \theta_c \), at which slipping is impending, satisfies \( \tan\theta_c = \mu_s \). The mass cancels: both the driving component \( mg\sin\theta \) and the friction limit \( \mu_s mg\cos\theta \) are proportional to \( m \), so a heavier block of the same material starts to slide at the same angle. This gives a method of measuring \( \mu_s \): tilt a board slowly until a block on it begins to slip, and \( \mu_s = \tan\theta_c \). Likewise, if a block, once started, slides at constant velocity at angle \( \theta \), then \( mg\sin\theta = \mu_k mg\cos\theta \) and \( \mu_k = \tan\theta \).

**Sliding down.** Kinetic friction acts up the slope, opposite the velocity:
\[ ma = mg\sin\theta - \mu_k mg\cos\theta \ \Rightarrow\ a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta) \ \ (\text{down the slope}). \]

**Sliding up.** A block moving up the slope, after being launched, has kinetic friction directed down the slope, the same way as the weight component:
\[ a = g(\sin\theta + \mu_k\cos\theta) \ \ (\text{directed down the slope, so the block slows}). \]
Friction reverses when the velocity reverses, so the two legs of a round trip have different accelerations. When the block stops at the top, it stays there if \( \tan\theta \le \mu_s \) and slides back otherwise.

**Worked example.** A block is launched at 6.00 m/s up a \( 30.0^\circ \) incline with \( \mu_k = 0.200 \) and \( \mu_s = 0.300 \).

1. Going up: \( a = 9.80(\sin 30.0^\circ + 0.200\cos 30.0^\circ) = 9.80(0.500 + 0.173) = 6.60 \) m/s², down the slope. Distance \( d = 6.00^2/(2 \times 6.60) = 2.73 \) m; time \( 6.00/6.60 = 0.909 \) s.
2. At the top: \( \tan 30.0^\circ = 0.577 > 0.300 \), so static friction cannot hold the block; it slides back.
3. Coming down: \( a = 9.80(0.500 - 0.173) = 3.20 \) m/s². Return speed \( \sqrt{2(3.20)(2.73)} = 4.18 \) m/s; time \( \sqrt{2(2.73)/3.20} = 1.31 \) s.

The block returns more slowly than it left and takes longer to come down than to go up, because friction opposes the motion on both legs.

**Common mistakes.** Using \( f_s = \mu_s N \) for a block at rest on an incline. Keeping the friction direction fixed when the velocity reverses. Applying \( a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta) \) to a block that is not sliding: if \( \tan\theta \le \mu_s \) a block at rest stays at rest, and the formula (which may even give a negative number) does not describe it.

questions.prompt: A block rests on a board whose angle is slowly increased. The coefficient of static friction is 0.350. At what angle, in degrees, does the block begin to slide?
questions.why: Impending motion: \( mg\sin\theta_c = \mu_s mg\cos\theta_c \), so \( \tan\theta_c = 0.350 \) and \( \theta_c = 19.3^\circ \), independent of the block's mass.

questions.prompt: A block slides down a \( 35.0^\circ \) incline with \( \mu_k = 0.250 \). Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², find the magnitude of its acceleration, in m/s².
questions.why: Friction acts up the slope: \( a = g(\sin 35.0^\circ - \mu_k\cos 35.0^\circ) = 9.80(0.574 - 0.205) = 3.61 \) m/s² down the slope.

options: \( \mu_s mg\cos\theta \)
\( mg\sin\theta \)
\( \mu_s mg \)
\( mg\cos\theta \)
questions.prompt: A block of mass \( m \) rests on an incline of angle \( \theta \), with static coefficient \( \mu_s \), and does not slip. What is the magnitude of the static friction force on it?
questions.why: At rest, the forces along the slope balance: \( f_s = mg\sin\theta \). Option 1 is the maximum static friction, reached only at impending motion. Option 3 also uses \( N = mg \), which is wrong on an incline. Option 4 is the normal force, confusing the perpendicular and parallel components.

sections.title: Inclines with friction

sections.md:
When a body on a rough surface is tied to another body, or rests on one, the direction of static friction depends on which way the system would move, and that has to be decided before any equation is written with a definite sign.

**Procedure.**

1. Ignore friction and find the direction in which the system tends to move, by comparing the forces that drive it along the rope.
2. Compare the net driving force with the largest static friction the surfaces can supply. If it is not larger, the system stays at rest and static friction balances it.
3. If it is larger, the system moves in the direction found in step 1, kinetic friction opposes that motion, and the second law for each body, with the rope constraint (equal magnitudes of acceleration), determines the motion.

**Worked example.** A 5.00 kg block sits on a \( 30.0^\circ \) incline with \( \mu_s = 0.400 \) and \( \mu_k = 0.300 \). A rope parallel to the incline runs from the block up over an ideal pulley at the top to a hanging mass \( m_2 \). Along the rope, the hanging mass pulls the block up the slope with \( m_2 g \) (when at rest), and the weight component \( m_1 g\sin\theta = 24.5 \) N pulls it down. The largest static friction is \( \mu_s m_1 g\cos\theta = 0.400(5.00)(9.80)(0.866) = 17.0 \) N.

(a) \( m_2 = 4.00 \) kg, released from rest: \( m_2 g = 39.2 \) N, so the tendency is for the block to move up the slope, with net driving force \( 39.2 - 24.5 = 14.7 \) N. Since \( 14.7 < 17.0 \), the system stays at rest, with 14.7 N of static friction directed down the slope and tension 39.2 N.

(b) \( m_2 = 5.00 \) kg: \( m_2 g = 49.0 \) N, net driving force \( 24.5 \) N \( > 17.0 \) N, so the block moves up the slope. Kinetic friction, \( \mu_k m_1 g\cos\theta = 12.7 \) N, points down the slope. With the block's positive direction up the slope and the hanging mass's positive direction down:
\[ T - m_1 g\sin\theta - f_k = m_1 a, \qquad m_2 g - T = m_2 a. \]
Adding, \( a = (49.0 - 24.5 - 12.7)/10.0 = 1.18 \) m/s², and \( T = m_2(g - a) = 5.00(9.80 - 1.18) = 43.1 \) N.

More generally, the system stays at rest for every \( m_2 \) between \( m_1(\sin\theta - \mu_s\cos\theta) = 0.768 \) kg and \( m_1(\sin\theta + \mu_s\cos\theta) = 4.23 \) kg; below that range the block slides down, above it up.

**Stacked bodies.** Friction also couples bodies resting on one another. A block of mass \( m \) sits on a block of mass \( M \), which lies on a frictionless floor, and a horizontal force \( F \) pulls the lower block. The only horizontal force on the upper block is static friction from the lower one, so here friction points forward, in the direction of motion. If the two move together, their common acceleration is \( a = F/(m + M) \), and the upper block needs \( f_s = ma \le \mu_s mg \), that is, \( a \le \mu_s g \). The largest force for which they move together is therefore
\[ F_{\max} = \mu_s(m + M)g. \]
For a larger force the upper block slides backward relative to the lower one, and kinetic friction then acts on both.

**Common mistakes.** Fixing the friction direction before finding the tendency. Using kinetic friction for a system that is actually at rest. Taking \( N = m_1 g \) for the block on the incline instead of \( m_1 g\cos\theta \).

questions.prompt: A 3.00 kg block on a horizontal table (\( \mu_k = 0.200 \)) is tied by an ideal rope over an ideal pulley to a hanging 2.00 kg block, and the system is moving. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², find the magnitude of the acceleration, in m/s².
questions.why: Table block: \( T - \mu_k m_1 g = m_1 a \). Hanging block: \( m_2 g - T = m_2 a \). Adding: \( a = (m_2 g - \mu_k m_1 g)/(m_1 + m_2) = (19.6 - 5.88)/5.00 = 2.74 \) m/s².

questions.model: Friction opposes relative sliding (or the tendency to slide), so its direction depends on which way the block would move, which is not known at the start. Step 1: ignore friction and compare the driving forces along the rope: the hanging weight \( m_2 g \) pulls the block up the slope, the component \( m_1 g\sin\theta \) pulls it down; the larger decides the tendency, and the difference is the net driving force. Step 2: find the largest available static friction, \( \mu_s m_1 g\cos\theta \). Step 3: if the net driving force does not exceed this, the system stays at rest and static friction equals the net driving force, pointing against the tendency; the tension is then \( m_2 g \). Step 4: otherwise the system accelerates in the tendency direction, kinetic friction \( \mu_k m_1 g\cos\theta \) points against the motion, and the two second-law equations with a common acceleration give \( a \) and \( T \).
questions.prompt: A block on a rough incline is connected over a pulley at the top to a hanging mass. Explain, as a step-by-step procedure, how to decide whether the system moves and in which direction, and why the direction of friction cannot be chosen at the outset.
rubric: Compare the driving forces along the rope without friction (m₂g versus m₁g sin θ) to find the tendency

sections.md:
A body moving through air or water experiences a resistive force, **drag**, that differs from kinetic friction in one essential way: it depends on the speed. This section sets up the equation of motion for a body falling with drag, solves it, and obtains the terminal speed.

**Drag models.** Drag points opposite to the body's velocity relative to the fluid, and its magnitude grows with speed. Two approximations cover most cases:

- **Linear drag**, \( f = bv \), for small, slow bodies in viscous fluids (fine dust in air, a bead sinking in oil). For a sphere of radius \( r \) in a fluid of viscosity \( \eta \), Stokes's law gives \( b = 6\pi\eta r \).
- **Quadratic drag**, \( f = Dv^2 \), for bodies of everyday size at everyday speeds in air, with \( D = \tfrac12 C\rho A \): \( \rho \) is the fluid density, \( A \) the cross-sectional area, and \( C \) a dimensionless drag coefficient set by the body's shape.

Which model applies depends on the size and speed of the body and on the fluid; both are approximations.

**Terminal speed.** A body dropped from rest has no drag at first and accelerates at \( g \). As its speed grows, the drag grows, the net force shrinks, and the acceleration falls toward zero. The speed approaches the **terminal speed** \( v_t \) at which drag balances the weight:
\[ \text{linear: } bv_t = mg \Rightarrow v_t = \frac{mg}{b}, \qquad \text{quadratic: } Dv_t^2 = mg \Rightarrow v_t = \sqrt{\frac{mg}{D}}. \]

**Solving the linear case.** Take down as positive. The second law is the differential equation
\[ m\frac{dv}{dt} = mg - bv, \]
with \( v(0) = 0 \). Separating variables,
\[ \int_0^v \frac{dv'}{mg - bv'} = \int_0^t \frac{dt'}{m} \quad\Rightarrow\quad -\frac1b\ln\frac{mg - bv}{mg} = \frac{t}{m}, \]
and solving for \( v \),
\[ v(t) = v_t\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right), \qquad \tau = \frac{m}{b}. \]
The **time constant** \( \tau \) sets the scale: after \( \tau \) the speed is \( (1 - e^{-1})v_t = 0.632\,v_t \), after \( 3\tau \) it is 95.0% of \( v_t \), and \( v_t \) is approached but never reached. Differentiating, \( a = g\,e^{-t/\tau} \): the acceleration starts at \( g \) and decays exponentially. Note also \( v_t = g\tau \). The quadratic equation \( m\,dv/dt = mg - Dv^2 \) is separable too; its solution from rest is \( v = v_t\tanh(gt/v_t) \).

**Worked example (linear drag).** A 0.200 kg object is dropped from rest, and the drag on it is modeled as linear with \( b = 0.0800 \) kg/s. Then \( \tau = 0.200/0.0800 = 2.50 \) s and \( v_t = mg/b = 24.5 \) m/s. At \( t = 2.50 \) s, \( v = 24.5(0.632) = 15.5 \) m/s, whereas without drag it would already be moving at 24.5 m/s. It reaches 90% of \( v_t \) when \( e^{-t/\tau} = 0.1 \), at \( t = \tau\ln 10 = 5.76 \) s.

**Worked example (quadratic drag).** A 75.0 kg skydiver falling belly-down has \( D \approx 0.250 \) kg/m. Then \( v_t = \sqrt{(75.0)(9.80)/0.250} = 54.2 \) m/s, about 195 km/h. Diving head-first reduces \( A \), hence \( D \), and raises \( v_t \).

In the plot, the rising curve is \( v(t) \) with linear drag (m/s, against \( t \) in s), the straight line is free fall without drag (its initial tangent), and the horizontal line is \( v_t = g\tau \). Drag the slider \( k \), the time constant \( \tau \) in seconds.

```plot
x: 0, 15
y: 0, 50
xlabel: t (s)
ylabel: v (m/s)
slider: k, 0.5, 5, 2.5 | τ (s)
f: 9.8*k*(1 - exp(-x/k)) | with linear drag
f: 9.8*x | no drag
hline: 9.8*k | terminal speed gτ
```

**Common mistakes.** Treating drag as a constant force and using constant-acceleration formulas. Carrying the vacuum result that all bodies fall alike into problems with drag: at equal shape and size, a heavier body has a larger terminal speed, since \( v_t = mg/b \) or \( \sqrt{mg/D} \).

questions.prompt: A body of mass \( m \) is dropped from rest and experiences linear drag \( bv \). Give its speed as a function of time \( t \), in terms of \( m \), \( g \), \( b \) and \( t \).
questions.why: Separate \( m\,dv/dt = mg - bv \): \( \int_0^v dv'/(mg - bv') = t/m \), so \( -\frac1b\ln\big(1 - bv/(mg)\big) = t/m \) and \( v = \dfrac{mg}{b}\big(1 - e^{-bt/m}\big) \).

questions.prompt: An 80.0 kg skydiver has quadratic drag coefficient \( D = 0.270 \) kg/m. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², find the terminal speed, in m/s.
questions.why: At terminal speed \( Dv_t^2 = mg \): \( v_t = \sqrt{784/0.270} = \sqrt{2904} = 53.9 \) m/s.

exam.prompt: A curve of radius 100 m is banked at \( 20.0^\circ \), and \( \mu_s = 0.300 \) between tires and road. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², find the greatest speed, in m/s, at which a car can take the curve without sliding.
exam.why: At the maximum speed friction acts down the slope at its limit. Vertical: \( N\cos\theta - \mu_s N\sin\theta = mg \). Horizontal: \( N\sin\theta + \mu_s N\cos\theta = mv^2/r \). Dividing: \( v^2 = rg\dfrac{\sin\theta + \mu_s\cos\theta}{\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta} = 980\dfrac{0.342 + 0.282}{0.940 - 0.103} = 730 \) m²/s², so \( v = 27.0 \) m/s (the frictionless design speed would be 18.9 m/s).

exam.model: Differentiate the unit vectors with the chain rule: \( \dfrac{d\hat r}{dt} = (-\sin\theta\,\hat\imath + \cos\theta\,\hat\jmath)\dot\theta = \dot\theta\,\hat\theta \) and \( \dfrac{d\hat\theta}{dt} = (-\cos\theta\,\hat\imath - \sin\theta\,\hat\jmath)\dot\theta = -\dot\theta\,\hat r \). With \( \vec r = r\hat r \) and \( r \) constant, \( \vec v = r\dot\theta\,\hat\theta \): tangent to the circle, with speed \( r|\dot\theta| \). Differentiating again, \( \vec a = r\ddot\theta\,\hat\theta + r\dot\theta\,\dfrac{d\hat\theta}{dt} = r\ddot\theta\,\hat\theta - r\dot\theta^2\,\hat r \). The component \( r\ddot\theta \) along \( \hat\theta \) is the tangential acceleration, equal to \( dv/dt \) for \( v = r\dot\theta \); the component \( -r\dot\theta^2 \) along \( \hat r \) points toward the center with magnitude \( r\dot\theta^2 = v^2/r \). For uniform motion \( \dot\theta = \omega \) is constant, \( \ddot\theta = 0 \), and \( \vec a = -r\omega^2\hat r = -\omega^2\vec r \), the centripetal acceleration \( v^2/r \) toward the center.
exam.prompt: A particle moves on a circle of radius \( r \) with angular position \( \theta(t) \), not necessarily at constant rate. Using the unit vectors \( \hat r = \cos\theta\,\hat\imath + \sin\theta\,\hat\jmath \) and \( \hat\theta = -\sin\theta\,\hat\imath + \cos\theta\,\hat\jmath \), derive the velocity and acceleration vectors, identify the tangential and centripetal components, and show that the uniform-motion result is a special case.

a = r θ̈ θ̂ − r θ̇² r̂: tangential r θ̈ = dv/dt, centripetal r θ̇² = v²/r toward the center
Uniform motion: θ̈ = 0, so a = −rω² r̂, magnitude v²/r toward the center
exam.why: The two terms separate the two ways a velocity can change: in magnitude (tangential) and in direction (centripetal).

exam.model: Two arrows are wrong. The 'centripetal force' is not a separate force but the name for the net inward force; here the only horizontal force is static friction from the road, and it is the centripetal force. The 'centrifugal force' has no agent in the ground frame, which is inertial, and must not be drawn. Drawn equal and opposite, the two invented arrows cancel and add nothing to the sum, but they suggest a balance of forces, as if the car were in equilibrium. It is not: it accelerates toward the center, so the net force must be nonzero and inward. Correct diagram: weight \( mg \) down, normal force \( N \) up, static friction \( f_s \) horizontal, toward the center. Vertical: \( N = mg \). Radial: \( f_s = mv^2/r \). The tires hold while \( f_s \le \mu_s N \), so \( mv^2/r \le \mu_s mg \), and \( v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s g r} \), independent of the car's mass.

'Centrifugal force' does not exist in the (inertial) ground frame; no body exerts it
Drawing the two as a balancing pair wrongly suggests equilibrium; the car accelerates toward the center, so the net force is nonzero and inward (friction)

exam.prompt: In an amusement-park rotor, riders stand against the inner wall of a vertical cylinder of radius 2.50 m, which spins with a period of 2.00 s; then the floor drops away. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², find the minimum coefficient of static friction between rider and wall that keeps the riders from sliding down.
exam.why: The wall's normal force points inward and is the centripetal force: \( N = m\omega^2 r = m(4\pi^2 r/T^2) \). Static friction, upward, must balance the weight: \( mg \le \mu_s N \). So \( \mu_s \ge \dfrac{gT^2}{4\pi^2 r} = \dfrac{9.80(4.00)}{4\pi^2(2.50)} = 0.397 \), independent of the rider's mass.

phy-0-4.intro:
A car rounding a bend, a stone whirled on a string, a centrifuge, and a point on a spinning wheel all move on circles, or on arcs that are circular over a short stretch. The speed may be constant, yet the velocity is not, because its direction turns continuously. By Newton's second law a changing velocity requires a net force. The questions of this chapter are therefore: what acceleration does motion on a circle require, and which forces provide it?

The first half answers the kinematic question. Differentiating the position of a particle on a circle shows that uniform circular motion has an acceleration of magnitude \( v^2/r \) directed toward the center, and that a changing speed adds a tangential component. The second half applies the second law along the radius to strings, road curves, banked tracks, conical pendulums and vertical loops, and explains why the outward "centrifugal force" of everyday speech has no place in an analysis made from an inertial frame.

practice.prompt: A 0.150 kg bob of a conical pendulum moves so that its string makes \( 40.0^\circ \) with the vertical. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², find the tension, in newtons.
practice.why: The vertical acceleration is zero: \( F_T\cos 40.0^\circ = mg \Rightarrow F_T = 1.47/0.766 = 1.92 \) N. The length of the string is not needed.

practice.prompt: A 60.0 kg rider passes the top of a vertical loop of radius 10.0 m at 12.0 m/s, upside down. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², find the normal force of the seat on the rider, in newtons.
practice.why: At the top both the weight and the normal force point down, toward the center: \( N + mg = mv^2/r \). \( N = 60.0(14.4) - 588 = 864 - 588 = 276 \) N.

practice.model: At the top, the water is acted on by its weight \( mg \), downward, and by the normal force \( N \) of the bucket's bottom. The bottom is on the outside of the circle, above the water, so it pushes the water downward, toward the center. The radial equation is \( N + mg = mv^2/r \). The water does accelerate downward, at \( v^2/r \); it stays in the bucket because at a sufficient speed the circular path requires a downward acceleration at least as large as \( g \), and the bucket supplies the difference by pushing down. The bucket can only push, so \( N \ge 0 \), which requires \( v^2/r \ge g \), i.e. \( v \ge \sqrt{gr} \). At a lower speed the path needs less downward acceleration than gravity alone produces; the water falls away from the bottom faster than the bucket's path curves, and it spills.
practice.prompt: A bucket of water is swung in a vertical circle of radius \( r \), and the water stays in even when the bucket is upside down at the top. Explain, with a free-body diagram of the water at the top, why it does not fall out, and find the minimum speed for this to work.
rubric: Forces on the water at the top: its weight and the push of the bucket bottom, both downward (toward the center)
Radial equation: N + mg = mv²/r
The water accelerates downward at v²/r; it stays on the circle if v²/r ≥ g, the bucket supplying the difference by pushing (N ≥ 0)
Minimum speed at the top √(gr); below it N would have to be negative (the bucket would need to pull), so the water leaves the circle
practice.why: The same inequality governs a roller coaster at the top of a loop and a ball on a string.

practice.prompt: A 1200 kg car passes over the crest of a hill of radius 30.0 m at 12.0 m/s. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², find the normal force of the road on the car, in newtons.
practice.why: The center is below: \( mg - N = mv^2/r \). \( N = 1200(9.80 - 4.80) = 6.00\times10^3 \) N, about 51% of the weight.

practice.model: (a) At the lowest point the string is vertical, the weight and tension are both vertical, and neither has a component along the path, so \( a_t = 0 \). The speed is greatest there and \( a_c = v^2/r \ne 0 \): the acceleration points straight up, toward the pivot. (b) At the turning point the bob is momentarily at rest, so \( a_c = v^2/r = 0 \). The weight has a component \( mg\sin\theta \) along the path (with \( \theta \) the string's angle from the vertical), so \( a_t = g\sin\theta \), directed along the arc back toward the lowest point. The acceleration is therefore tangent to the circle, perpendicular to the string. In between, both components are present and the acceleration points neither to the center nor along the path.
practice.prompt: A pendulum bob swings through the bottom of its arc and rises toward one end. Describe the direction of its acceleration (a) at the lowest point and (b) at the highest point of the swing, where it is momentarily at rest. Justify each answer with the tangential and centripetal components.
rubric: (a) At the lowest point the tangential component of gravity is zero, so aₜ = 0; the acceleration is v²/r, straight up toward the pivot
(b) At the end point v = 0, so the centripetal component v²/r is zero
(b) The tangential component g sin θ (θ from vertical) is nonzero, so the acceleration is tangent to the arc, directed back toward the lowest point
The acceleration points toward the center only where aₜ = 0
practice.why: Only in uniform circular motion does the acceleration point at the center; a pendulum is nonuniform circular motion.

phy-0-4.scope: Kinematics of motion on a circle (angular position, angular speed, period, frequency), the centripetal acceleration derived by differentiation, nonuniform circular motion with tangential and centripetal components, the second law along the radius, the fictitious centrifugal force, strings, conical pendulums, flat and banked curves, and vertical circles at their top and bottom; rigid-body rotation and torque belong to the rotation chapters, orbits to Gravitation and orbits, and speeds found from energy to the energy chapters.

sections.md:
This section sets up the quantities used to describe motion on a circle: angular position, angular speed, period and frequency. Everything later in the chapter is expressed through them.

**Angular position and arc length.** A particle moving on a circle of radius \( r \) centered at the origin is located by its **angular position** \( \theta \), measured counterclockwise from the \( +x \)-axis:
\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta. \]
With \( \theta \) in radians, the arc length from the \( +x \)-axis is \( s = r\theta \). This is in fact the definition of the **radian** (the angle whose arc equals the radius, so a full turn is \( 2\pi \) rad), and it is why radians, not degrees, appear in every formula below.

**Angular velocity.** The rate of change of the angular position, \( d\theta/dt \), is the **angular velocity**, measured in rad/s; its magnitude \( \omega = |d\theta/dt| \) is the angular speed. Differentiating \( s = r\theta \) with \( r \) constant gives the speed along the circle:
\[ v = \left|\frac{ds}{dt}\right| = r\left|\frac{d\theta}{dt}\right| = r\omega. \]

**Uniform circular motion.** Motion on a circle at constant speed is **uniform circular motion**, and then, for counterclockwise motion, \( \theta = \theta_0 + \omega t \). The **period** \( T \) is the time for one revolution, and the **frequency** \( f = 1/T \) is the number of revolutions per unit time, measured in hertz (1 Hz = 1 s⁻¹). One revolution is \( 2\pi \) rad and a distance \( 2\pi r \), so
\[ v = \frac{2\pi r}{T} = 2\pi r f, \qquad \omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi f. \]
Rotation rates are often quoted in revolutions per minute (rpm); dividing by 60 gives revolutions per second, that is, hertz.

**Worked example.** A laboratory centrifuge spins at 3000 rpm, and a sample sits 0.100 m from the axis.

1. Frequency: \( f = 3000/60 = 50.0 \) Hz; period \( T = 1/f = 0.0200 \) s.
2. Angular speed: \( \omega = 2\pi(50.0) = 314 \) rad/s.
3. Speed of the sample: \( v = r\omega = (0.100)(314) = 31.4 \) m/s.

All points of a rigid rotating body share the same \( \omega \), but each point's speed \( v = r\omega \) is proportional to its distance from the axis: a point halfway out moves at half the speed. Rigid-body rotation is developed in a later chapter; here each point is treated as a particle on its own circle.

**Common mistakes.** Using degrees in \( s = r\theta \) or \( v = r\omega \). Confusing the frequency \( f \) (revolutions per second) with the angular speed \( \omega \) (radians per second), which differ by the factor \( 2\pi \). Forgetting to convert rpm to revolutions per second before using \( \omega = 2\pi f \).

questions.prompt: A wheel of radius 0.350 m turns at 480 rpm. Find the speed of a point on its rim, in m/s.
A point at distance \( r \) from an axis rotates at \( n \) revolutions per minute (type `n`). Give its speed in terms of \( r \) and \( n \), in units consistent with \( r \) per second.
questions.why: Frequency in hertz: \( f = n/60 \). Speed: \( v = 2\pi r f = 2\pi r n/60 = \pi r n/30 \).

sections.title: Describing motion on a circle

sections.md:
In uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the direction of the velocity changes continually, so the particle accelerates. This section finds that acceleration by differentiating the position vector.

**Derivation.** For uniform circular motion starting on the \( +x \)-axis, \( \theta = \omega t \) and
\[ \vec r(t) = r\cos(\omega t)\,\hat\imath + r\sin(\omega t)\,\hat\jmath. \]
Differentiating component by component, as in the chapter on projectile motion,
\[ \vec v = \frac{d\vec r}{dt} = -r\omega\sin(\omega t)\,\hat\imath + r\omega\cos(\omega t)\,\hat\jmath, \]
\[ \vec a = \frac{d\vec v}{dt} = -r\omega^2\cos(\omega t)\,\hat\imath - r\omega^2\sin(\omega t)\,\hat\jmath = -\omega^2\,\vec r. \]
Three facts follow. First, \( |\vec v| = r\omega \), confirming \( v = r\omega \). Second, \( \vec v\cdot\vec r = 0 \): the velocity is perpendicular to the radius, that is, tangent to the circle. Third, \( \vec a = -\omega^2\vec r \) points from the particle toward the center, with magnitude
\[ a_c = \omega^2 r = \frac{v^2}{r} = \frac{4\pi^2 r}{T^2}. \]
This is the **centripetal acceleration** (from the Latin for "center-seeking"). It is present whenever a particle moves on a circle, even at constant speed, because acceleration measures every change of the velocity vector, including a change of direction.

**A geometric check.** In a short time \( \Delta t \) the position vector turns through an angle \( \Delta\theta \), and the velocity vector, always perpendicular to it, turns through the same angle. The triangle formed by \( \vec r_1 \), \( \vec r_2 \) and \( \Delta\vec r \) and the triangle formed by \( \vec v_1 \), \( \vec v_2 \) and \( \Delta\vec v \) are therefore similar isosceles triangles, so \( |\Delta\vec v|/v = |\Delta\vec r|/r \). Dividing by \( \Delta t \) and letting \( \Delta t \to 0 \), with \( |\Delta\vec r|/\Delta t \to v \), gives \( a = v^2/r \) again.

The plot shows a circle of unit radius (arbitrary units) with the velocity at \( 45^\circ \), tangent to the circle, and the acceleration, pointing to the center.

```plot
x: -2, 2
y: -1.18, 1.18
param: cos(t); sin(t) | path
t: 0, 6.2832
vector: (0.7071, 0.7071) -> (0.4243, 0.9899) | v
vector: (0.7071, 0.7071) -> (0.4243, 0.4243) | a
point: 0, 0 | center
```

**Worked example 1.** A car takes a curve of radius 50.0 m at a constant 15.0 m/s. Its acceleration is \( v^2/r = 225/50.0 = 4.50 \) m/s², directed toward the center of the curve: almost half of \( g \), although the speedometer reading never changes.

**Worked example 2.** A point on Earth's equator is carried around a circle of radius \( 6.37\times10^6 \) m once per sidereal day, 86 164 s. Then \( \omega = 2\pi/86\,164 = 7.29\times10^{-5} \) rad/s, \( v = r\omega = 465 \) m/s, and \( a_c = \omega^2 r = 0.0339 \) m/s², about 0.35% of \( g \). This small value is what justifies treating the ground as an inertial frame.

**Common mistakes.** Concluding that a body moving at constant speed has zero acceleration. Pointing the acceleration along the velocity, or outward. Using a diameter in place of the radius in \( v^2/r \).

questions.prompt: A point on the rim of a wheel of radius 0.300 m turns at 1200 rpm. Find the magnitude of its centripetal acceleration, in m/s².

questions.model: Differentiating componentwise: \( \vec v = -r\omega\sin(\omega t)\,\hat\imath + r\omega\cos(\omega t)\,\hat\jmath \). Its magnitude is \( r\omega\sqrt{\sin^2 + \cos^2} = r\omega \), and \( \vec v\cdot\vec r = r^2\omega(-\cos\sin + \sin\cos) = 0 \), so the velocity is perpendicular to the radius, i.e. tangent to the circle. Differentiating again: \( \vec a = -r\omega^2\cos(\omega t)\,\hat\imath - r\omega^2\sin(\omega t)\,\hat\jmath = -\omega^2\vec r \), which is antiparallel to the position vector measured from the center, so it points toward the center, with magnitude \( \omega^2 r = (v/r)^2 r = v^2/r \). The particle accelerates because acceleration is the rate of change of the velocity vector, and although \( |\vec v| \) is constant, the direction of \( \vec v \) rotates continuously.
questions.prompt: Starting from \( \vec r(t) = r\cos(\omega t)\,\hat\imath + r\sin(\omega t)\,\hat\jmath \), derive the velocity and acceleration of a particle in uniform circular motion. Show that the velocity is tangent to the circle, that the acceleration points to the center, and that its magnitude is \( v^2/r \). Explain why the particle accelerates although its speed is constant.
rubric: v = rω(−sin ωt î + cos ωt ĵ), with |v| = rω and v·r = 0 (tangent)
a = −rω²(cos ωt î + sin ωt ĵ) = −ω² r, pointing toward the center
|a| = ω²r = v²/r using v = rω
Acceleration is the rate of change of the velocity vector; its direction changes continuously even though its magnitude does not
questions.why: The result \( \vec a = -\omega^2\vec r \) holds at every instant, not only at the starting point.

options: There is no acceleration, because the speed is constant.
North, along the velocity.
West, toward the center.
East, away from the center.
questions.prompt: A stone is whirled at constant speed in a horizontal circle. At the instant shown it is moving north, and the center of the circle is to its west. What is the direction of its acceleration?
questions.why: In uniform circular motion the acceleration is \( v^2/r \) toward the center: west. Option 1 confuses constant speed with constant velocity. Option 2 treats acceleration as parallel to velocity, true only for straight-line motion. Option 4 reflects the idea of a centrifugal effect; in an inertial frame nothing accelerates the stone outward.

sections.title: Centripetal acceleration

sections.md:
When the speed along the circle changes, as for a car accelerating out of a bend or a ball swinging on a string, the acceleration acquires a second component. This section derives both components for arbitrary motion on a circle.

**Derivation.** Let \( \theta(t) \) be any twice-differentiable function, and write a dot for \( d/dt \). Define the unit vectors
\[ \hat r = \cos\theta\,\hat\imath + \sin\theta\,\hat\jmath \ \ (\text{outward along the radius}), \qquad \hat\theta = -\sin\theta\,\hat\imath + \cos\theta\,\hat\jmath \ \ (\text{tangent, toward increasing } \theta). \]
They depend on time through \( \theta \); by the chain rule, \( d\hat r/dt = \dot\theta\,\hat\theta \) and \( d\hat\theta/dt = -\dot\theta\,\hat r \). With \( \vec r = r\hat r \) and \( r \) constant, differentiating twice gives
\[ \vec v = r\dot\theta\,\hat\theta, \qquad \vec a = r\ddot\theta\,\hat\theta - r\dot\theta^{2}\,\hat r. \]
Write \( v = r\dot\theta \) for the velocity component along \( \hat\theta \) (the speed, for counterclockwise motion), and note that \( \dot\theta^{2} = \omega^2 \). The acceleration has two perpendicular parts:
\[ a_t = r\ddot\theta = \frac{dv}{dt} \ \ (\text{tangential}), \qquad a_c = r\omega^2 = \frac{v^2}{r} \ \ (\text{toward the center}). \]
The **tangential acceleration** changes the speed; the centripetal part changes the direction. Because they are perpendicular, the magnitude of the acceleration is
\[ a = \sqrt{a_t^2 + a_c^2}. \]
Uniform circular motion is the special case \( a_t = 0 \). The same decomposition holds at any point of any smooth curved path, with \( r \) replaced by the **radius of curvature**, the radius of the circle that best fits the path there.

**Worked example.** A car starts from rest on a circular track of radius 80.0 m and speeds up with constant tangential acceleration 2.00 m/s². Find its acceleration at \( t = 5.00 \) s.

1. Speed: \( v = a_t t = 10.0 \) m/s.
2. Centripetal component: \( a_c = v^2/r = 100/80.0 = 1.25 \) m/s².
3. Magnitude: \( a = \sqrt{2.00^2 + 1.25^2} = 2.36 \) m/s², directed \( \arctan(1.25/2.00) = 32.0^\circ \) from the velocity, toward the inside of the curve.

The tangential component stays fixed while the centripetal one grows as \( t^2 \). They are equal when \( v^2 = r a_t = 160 \) m²/s², at \( v = 12.6 \) m/s and \( t = 6.32 \) s. By the second law the net force on the car points the same way as its acceleration: partly forward and partly inward, not toward the center.

**Common mistakes.** Using \( v^2/r \) as the whole acceleration when the speed is changing. Adding the components as numbers (\( 2.00 + 1.25 \)) instead of in quadrature. Believing that the acceleration in circular motion always points to the center; it does so only when the speed is constant.

questions.prompt: A car travels around a curve of radius 60.0 m. At the instant its speed is 12.0 m/s, it is braking with a tangential deceleration of 3.00 m/s². Find the magnitude of its total acceleration, in m/s².
questions.why: \( a_c = v^2/r = 144/60.0 = 2.40 \) m/s² (inward), \( a_t = 3.00 \) m/s² (backward along the path). Perpendicular, so \( a = \sqrt{3.00^2 + 2.40^2} = 3.84 \) m/s².

questions.prompt: A particle moves on a circle of radius 2.00 m with angular position \( \theta(t) = bt^2 \), where \( b = 0.500 \) rad/s². Find the magnitude of its acceleration at \( t = 2.00 \) s, in m/s².
questions.why: \( \dot\theta = 2bt = 2.00 \) rad/s and \( \ddot\theta = 2b = 1.00 \) rad/s² at \( t = 2.00 \) s. \( a_t = R\ddot\theta = 2.00 \) m/s², \( a_c = R\dot\theta^2 = 2.00(4.00) = 8.00 \) m/s². \( a = \sqrt{2.00^2 + 8.00^2} = 8.25 \) m/s². In general \( a = 2bR\sqrt{1 + 4b^2t^4} \): the centripetal part grows as \( t^2 \) and soon dominates.

sections.title: Nonuniform circular motion

sections.md:
Kinematics says what acceleration a circular path requires; the second law says what net force it takes. This section states the radial form of the second law, applies it, and clears up the most persistent misconception in the subject. In this chapter tension is written \( F_T \), to keep \( T \) for the period.

**The radial equation.** Resolve the forces into a component toward the center and a tangential component. The second law gives
\[ \sum F_{\text{in}} = m\frac{v^2}{r}, \qquad \sum F_t = m\frac{dv}{dt}. \]
In uniform circular motion the tangential sum is zero and the net force points exactly toward the center, with magnitude \( mv^2/r \). The name **centripetal force** describes this role, not a new kind of force: the inward net force is supplied by forces already known, such as tension, gravity, a normal force or friction. On a free-body diagram you draw those forces, set their inward sum equal to \( mv^2/r \), and never add an extra arrow labeled "centripetal force".

**No centrifugal force in an inertial frame.** A passenger in a car turning left feels pressed against the right-hand door, and it is tempting to say that an outward "centrifugal force" pushes her. In the ground frame no body exerts such a force. By the first law she tends to continue in a straight line; the car turns left beneath her until the door reaches her and pushes her inward, to the left, supplying her centripetal force. Similarly, if the string of a whirled stone breaks, the stone does not fly radially outward: with no horizontal force acting, it moves off along the tangent, in the direction of its velocity at that instant. In the rotating frame of the car one can introduce a fictitious outward force of magnitude \( mv^2/r \) to make Newton's laws appear to hold, but it has no agent and no third-law partner. All analysis in this course is done in inertial frames, where it does not appear.

**Worked example (string on a table).** A 0.250 kg puck on a frictionless horizontal table is tied by a 0.800 m string to a peg and makes 2.00 revolutions per second. The vertical forces (weight and normal force) balance, and the only horizontal force is the tension, directed toward the peg:
\[ F_T = m\omega^2 r = (0.250)(2\pi \times 2.00)^2(0.800) = 31.6\ \text{N}. \]
Because \( F_T \propto \omega^2 \), doubling the rotation rate quadruples the tension.

**Worked example (conical pendulum).** A 0.200 kg bob on a string of length \( L = 1.00 \) m moves in a horizontal circle, with the string at \( \beta = 30.0^\circ \) to the vertical. This arrangement is a **conical pendulum**. The circle has radius \( r = L\sin\beta = 0.500 \) m and its center is directly below the support, so the acceleration is horizontal. Forces: weight \( mg \) down and tension \( F_T \) along the string. With horizontal (toward the center) and vertical axes,
\[ \text{vertical: } F_T\cos\beta = mg, \qquad \text{horizontal: } F_T\sin\beta = \frac{mv^2}{r}. \]

1. Tension: \( F_T = mg/\cos\beta = 1.96/0.866 = 2.26 \) N.
2. Dividing the equations, \( \tan\beta = v^2/(rg) \), so \( v = \sqrt{rg\tan\beta} = \sqrt{(0.500)(9.80)(0.577)} = 1.68 \) m/s.
3. Period: writing \( v = \omega r \) with \( r = L\sin\beta \), the horizontal equation becomes \( F_T = m\omega^2 L \); combined with the vertical one, \( \omega^2 = g/(L\cos\beta) \), so \( T = 2\pi\sqrt{L\cos\beta/g} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.866/9.80} = 1.87 \) s, independent of the mass.

**Common mistakes.** Adding "centripetal force" as an extra force on the diagram. Drawing an outward centrifugal force in an inertial-frame analysis. Tilting the axes along the string in the conical pendulum: the acceleration is horizontal, so horizontal and vertical axes give one equation with zero acceleration.

questions.prompt: A 0.300 kg puck on a frictionless horizontal table moves in a circle on a 0.600 m string at 1.50 revolutions per second. Find the tension in the string, in newtons.
questions.why: \( \omega = 2\pi(1.50) = 9.42 \) rad/s. The tension is the only horizontal force: \( F_T = m\omega^2 r = 0.300(88.8)(0.600) = 16.0 \) N.

questions.model: (a) Seen from above, the stone leaves along the tangent to the circle at the point where the string broke, moving in the direction of its velocity at that instant; it does not move radially outward. (It also begins to fall, as a projectile.) (b) While the string was intact, the only horizontal force on the stone was the tension, pointing inward and supplying the centripetal force \( mv^2/r \) that kept turning its velocity. When the string breaks, that inward force disappears. With no horizontal force, the first law says the stone's horizontal velocity stays constant, and that velocity was tangent to the circle. Nothing pushed the stone outward: no body exerts such a force, and it would have no third-law partner. The 'centrifugal force' arises only if one describes the motion from the rotating frame of the string, which is not inertial.
questions.prompt: A stone is whirled in a horizontal circle on a string, and the string breaks. (a) Describe the stone's path immediately afterward, as seen from above. (b) A classmate explains the event by saying 'the centrifugal force threw it outward'. Explain, from an inertial frame, what actually happened and why no outward force was involved.
rubric: (a) It moves off along the tangent to the circle at the release point (then falls as a projectile), not radially outward
(b) Before the break the tension pulled the stone inward, supplying the centripetal force mv²/r
When the string breaks the inward force vanishes; with no horizontal force the stone keeps its velocity (first law), which was tangent
No body exerts an outward force; 'centrifugal force' is a fictitious force that appears only in the rotating frame
questions.why: The absence of an outward force is visible in the path: a radially outward escape would require a radial push.

questions.prompt: A conical pendulum has a string 1.50 m long that makes \( 25.0^\circ \) with the vertical. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², find its period, in seconds.

sections.title: Forces in circular motion

sections.md:
A car cannot turn unless something pushes it toward the center of the curve. On a level road that something is friction; on a banked road the normal force helps. This section finds the speeds each arrangement can handle.

**Level curve.** A car of mass \( m \) rounds a level curve of radius \( r \) at constant speed \( v \). The forces are its weight, the normal force, and friction from the road. The tires roll without skidding, so the friction is static, and since the speed is constant it points toward the center, perpendicular to the velocity. Vertically, \( N = mg \); radially, \( f_s = mv^2/r \). The tires hold if \( f_s \le \mu_s N \):
\[ \frac{mv^2}{r} \le \mu_s mg \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v \le v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s g r}. \]
The mass cancels: a truck and a small car with equally good tires have the same limiting speed. With \( r = 50.0 \) m and \( \mu_s = 0.800 \) (dry pavement), \( v_{\max} = \sqrt{0.800 \times 9.80 \times 50.0} = 19.8 \) m/s, about 71 km/h; on a wet road with \( \mu_s = 0.400 \), 14.0 m/s. Halving \( \mu_s \) lowers the safe speed by the factor \( \sqrt2 \), not 2.

**Banked curve without friction.** Tilting the roadway by an angle \( \theta \) toward the center tilts the normal force inward, so that its horizontal component can supply the centripetal force. The car moves in a horizontal circle, so its acceleration \( v^2/r \) is horizontal. Choose horizontal (toward the center) and vertical axes, not axes along the road surface as on an inclined plane. With no friction,
\[ \text{vertical: } N\cos\theta = mg, \qquad \text{horizontal: } N\sin\theta = \frac{mv^2}{r}, \]
and dividing,
\[ \tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg}. \]
This is the **ideal banking angle** for speed \( v \): at that speed no friction is needed at all. For a curve of radius 120 m designed for 25.0 m/s, \( \tan\theta = 625/(120 \times 9.80) = 0.531 \), so \( \theta = 28.0^\circ \). Note that \( N = mg/\cos\theta = 1.13\,mg \): on a banked curve the normal force exceeds the weight, the reverse of the inclined plane, because here it must also provide the horizontal acceleration.

In the plot, the curve is the ideal banking angle (degrees) against speed (m/s). Drag the slider \( k \), the radius in meters, and watch how a tighter curve needs a steeper bank for the same speed.

```plot
x: 0, 40
y: 0, 80
xlabel: v (m/s)
ylabel: θ (degrees)
slider: k, 20, 300, 120 | radius r (m)
f: atan(x^2/(9.8*k))*180/pi | ideal banking angle
```

**Banked curve with friction.** Above the design speed, friction must act down the slope to add inward force; below it, friction acts up the slope to keep the car from sliding inward and down. With friction at its limit \( \mu_s N \) directed down the slope, the equations become \( N\cos\theta - \mu_s N\sin\theta = mg \) and \( N\sin\theta + \mu_s N\cos\theta = mv^2/r \), and dividing,
\[ v_{\max}^2 = rg\,\frac{\sin\theta + \mu_s\cos\theta}{\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta}. \]
The minimum speed follows by reversing the friction, which amounts to replacing \( \mu_s \) by \( -\mu_s \).

**Common mistakes.** Treating the friction on a turning car as kinetic; tires that are not skidding are held by static friction. Resolving along the banked surface and setting the acceleration along it to zero: the acceleration is horizontal and nonzero. Writing \( N = mg\cos\theta \) on a banked curve by analogy with the incline.

questions.prompt: What is the greatest speed, in m/s, at which a car can round a level curve of radius 80.0 m if \( \mu_s = 0.600 \) between tires and road? Use \( g = 9.80 \) m/s².
questions.why: Static friction supplies the centripetal force: \( mv^2/r \le \mu_s mg \), so \( v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s g r} = \sqrt{0.600(9.80)(80.0)} = \sqrt{470} = 21.7 \) m/s.

questions.prompt: Find the ideal banking angle, in degrees, for a curve of radius 200 m designed for 30.0 m/s. Use \( g = 9.80 \) m/s².

questions.model: The student has copied the inclined-plane analysis, in which the body slides along the surface or rests. On the banked curve the car moves in a horizontal circle, so its acceleration is \( v^2/r \), horizontal and toward the center. This acceleration has a component along the banked surface (toward the inside, down the slope), so setting the along-surface acceleration to zero is wrong. The clean choice is horizontal and vertical axes, because then the vertical acceleration is zero: \( N\cos\theta = mg \) and \( N\sin\theta = mv^2/r \), giving \( N = mg/\cos\theta \) and \( \tan\theta = v^2/(rg) \). The normal force exceeds the weight because only its vertical component, \( N\cos\theta \), balances the weight, while it must also have a horizontal component to supply the centripetal force.
questions.prompt: For a car on a frictionless banked curve, a student resolves forces along and perpendicular to the road surface, as for a block on an inclined plane, sets the acceleration along the surface to zero, and concludes that \( N = mg\cos\theta \). Identify the error, give the correct analysis, and explain why the normal force on the banked curve exceeds the weight.
rubric: The car's acceleration is v²/r horizontally toward the center, not zero along the surface; its component along the slope is not zero
Correct axes: horizontal (toward center) and vertical, since the acceleration is horizontal
N cos θ = mg and N sin θ = mv²/r, so N = mg/cos θ and tan θ = v²/(rg)
N > mg because its vertical component alone must balance the weight, while it also has a horizontal component
questions.why: Choose axes so that one of them lies along the acceleration; on a banked curve that direction is horizontal.

sections.md:
Motion in a vertical circle, such as a ball whirled on a string, a car in a loop, or a car over the crest of a hill, adds gravity to the forces along the radius. At most points gravity also has a tangential component, so the speed changes and the motion is nonuniform. The radial equation of the previous section still holds at every instant, with the speed at that instant; this section applies it at the top and the bottom, where the forces are simplest. How the speed varies around the circle is most easily found with energy methods, developed in the following chapters; here the speeds are given.

**A ball on a string.** At each point, take the direction toward the center as positive in \( \sum F_{\text{in}} = mv^2/r \).

- At the bottom, the tension points up, toward the center, and the weight points away from it: \( F_T - mg = mv^2/r \), so \( F_T = mg + mv^2/r \). The string must hold up the ball and also supply the centripetal force, so the tension is greatest here, and this is where a string is most likely to break.
- At the top, both forces point down, toward the center: \( F_T + mg = mv^2/r \), so \( F_T = mv^2/r - mg \).

A string can only pull, so \( F_T \ge 0 \) at the top requires
\[ v_{\text{top}} \ge \sqrt{gr}. \]
At exactly this speed gravity alone supplies the centripetal force. At a lower speed the weight would exceed the inward force that circular motion at that speed requires; the string goes slack before the top, and the ball leaves the circle on a projectile path. The same condition, with the track's normal force in place of the tension, gives the minimum speed at the top of a roller-coaster loop.

**Worked example.** A 0.500 kg ball is whirled in a vertical circle on a 1.20 m string.

1. At the top, moving at 4.00 m/s: \( F_T = (0.500)(4.00)^2/1.20 - (0.500)(9.80) = 6.67 - 4.90 = 1.77 \) N.
2. Minimum speed at the top: \( \sqrt{(9.80)(1.20)} = 3.43 \) m/s.
3. At the bottom, moving at 7.00 m/s: \( F_T = 4.90 + (0.500)(49.0)/1.20 = 4.90 + 20.4 = 25.3 \) N, about five times the ball's weight.

**Over the crest of a hill.** A car passing over a rounded crest of radius \( r \) moves on the outside of the circle, whose center is below it. The weight points toward the center and the normal force away from it:
\[ mg - N = \frac{mv^2}{r} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad N = m\left(g - \frac{v^2}{r}\right). \]
The road pushes up with less than the car's weight, so the occupants' apparent weight is reduced. At \( v = \sqrt{gr} \), \( N = 0 \) and the car loses contact with the road; faster than that, it leaves the road. For a crest of radius 40.0 m the limit is 19.8 m/s, and at 15.0 m/s the apparent weight is \( 1 - 225/392 = 0.426 \) of the true weight.

**Inside a loop.** At the top of a loop the rider is upside down, with the track's normal force and the weight both pointing down, toward the center: \( N + mg = mv^2/r \). The rider is pressed into the seat with \( N = m(v^2/r - g) \), which can exceed \( mg \) if \( v^2 > 2gr \).

**Common mistakes.** Using a fixed "up is positive" convention and then writing \( mv^2/r \) with the wrong sign at the top; take the direction toward the center as positive at each point. Assuming the tension is the same all around the circle. Treating \( \sqrt{gr} \) as a minimum speed at the bottom; it is the condition at the top.

questions.prompt: A roller coaster car goes around the inside of a vertical loop of radius 6.00 m. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², what is the minimum speed at the top, in m/s, for the car to stay on the track without any restraint?
questions.why: At the top \( N + mg = mv^2/r \) with \( N \ge 0 \), so \( v \ge \sqrt{gr} = \sqrt{58.8} = 7.67 \) m/s.

questions.prompt: A 0.400 kg ball swings in a vertical circle on a 0.900 m string and passes the lowest point at 5.00 m/s. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², find the tension there, in newtons.
questions.why: At the bottom, toward the center (up) is positive: \( F_T - mg = mv^2/r \). \( F_T = 3.92 + 0.400(25.0)/0.900 = 3.92 + 11.1 = 15.0 \) N.

questions.model: At the crest the car moves on a circle whose center is below it. The weight \( mg \) points down, toward the center; the normal force \( N \) points up, away from it. The radial equation, with 'toward the center' positive, is \( mg - N = mv^2/r \), so \( N = m(g - v^2/r) \). Since \( N < mg \), the seat pushes on the passengers with less than their weight (each passenger obeys the same equation), and they feel lighter. The road can only push, so \( N \ge 0 \), which requires \( v \le \sqrt{gr} \). At \( v = \sqrt{gr} \) gravity alone supplies the needed centripetal force and \( N = 0 \); at a greater speed even gravity is not enough to bend the path to radius \( r \), so the car leaves the road. The mass cancels, so the critical speed is the same for every car.
questions.prompt: A car drives over the rounded crest of a hill of radius \( r \) at speed \( v \). Derive the normal force on the car at the top, explain why the passengers feel lighter, and find the speed at which the car leaves the road. Does the answer depend on the car's mass?
rubric: Center of the circle is below; weight points toward it, normal force away from it
mg − N = mv²/r, so N = m(g − v²/r) < mg: apparent weight reduced
N = 0 at v = √(gr); above that speed the road cannot hold the car on the circle, so it leaves the road
Independent of mass (m cancels)
questions.why: This is the outside-of-the-circle counterpart of the top of a loop.

ω = dθ/dt, in rad/s; for motion on a circle the speed is v = rω.

The time T for one revolution; T = 2πr/v = 2π/ω.
Revolutions per unit time, f = 1/T, in hertz; ω = 2πf.
The acceleration toward the center of the circle, of magnitude v²/r = ω²r, present whenever a path curves.
The component of acceleration along the velocity, aₜ = dv/dt; it changes the speed.
The radius of the circle that best fits a curved path at a point; the centripetal acceleration there is v² divided by it.
The name for the net inward force mv²/r in circular motion, supplied by real forces such as tension, gravity, normal force or friction; not a separate force.
A fictitious outward force introduced in a rotating (non-inertial) frame; it has no agent and does not appear in inertial-frame analysis.
A bob moving in a horizontal circle on a string that sweeps out a cone; tan β = v²/(rg), period 2π√(L cos β/g).
